speaker: Tri Dao
title: Tri Dao: The End of Nvidia's Dominance, Why Inference Costs Fell & The Next 10X in Speed
question: In AI chip design, why are multi-year hardware bets still risky even though models appear to have converged on Transformers?
guest: On the architecture side, from a very high level, it looks like it has sort of stabilized around the Transformer. But once you look a little bit closer, there's actually quite a bit of change around that. The most recent one in the last couple years has been Mixture of Experts, where you make the model much larger with many more parameters, but sparser. That has certain trade-offs: you need more memory, but maybe the amount of compute you do is a little bit smaller. Even that presents difficulty for some chip makers, because maybe they were designing for a dense model where it's very uniform compute, and now you have something sparse, so it's harder to design for. Similarly, attention has been around for ten-plus years, but there are changes here and there that actually make this stuff difficult. For example, DeepSeek has multi-head latent attention, which looks a little bit different from standard attention—they have a very large head dimension, and if your systolic array, the matrix multiplication engine, has a certain fixed size, maybe it doesn't fit.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because "Transformer" names a broad family, not a fixed workload, and a chip takes two to three years to design and then must earn its keep for several more. Over that span, the things hardware actually optimizes for keep shifting beneath the stable architectural label.

The operator mix changes: attention variants, state-space or diffusion hybrids, mixture-of-experts routing, and new normalization or activation functions can strand fixed-function logic. Numerical formats move too, from FP16 to INT8 to 4-bit and lower quantization. The balance of compute, memory capacity and memory bandwidth swings with context lengths, KV caching, and model size, so a chip tuned for one ratio may be bottlenecked on another. Workload shape also shifts, for instance from training to inference, from batch throughput to low-latency agentic and reasoning-heavy serving, or from datacenter to edge.

Specialization buys efficiency only by baking in assumptions, so the more a design bets on today's Transformer, the worse it fares if those assumptions drift. Meanwhile, general-purpose GPUs improve yearly and carry a mature software ecosystem, which narrows the window in which a specialized chip can pay off.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Custom silicon takes three to five years from architectural freeze to deployment, whereas the "Transformer" label masks rapid, hardware-breaking shifts in compute, memory, and networking bottlenecks. Within Transformers, dense models have largely yielded to sparse Mixture-of-Experts designs that trade raw FLOPs for vast memory capacity and low-latency all-to-all interconnects. Attention mechanisms also mutate constantly—from standard multi-head to grouped-query, latent, linear, and hybrid state-space variants—repeatedly shifting bottlenecks among HBM bandwidth, on-chip SRAM, and matrix engines. Simultaneously, numerical precision keeps dropping from 16-bit to 8-bit and microscaled 4-bit formats, stranding fixed-function datapaths chosen years earlier. Workload dynamics change just as fast: reasoning chains, test-time scaling, speculative decoding, reinforcement learning rollouts, and long-context agents radically alter batch sizes, KV-cache pressure, and prefill-to-decode ratios. Because algorithms evolve far faster than tape-out cycles—and post-Transformer paradigms could still emerge—over-specialized chips risk arriving obsolete compared to more general, programmable accelerators backed by mature software stacks.
